chunks: "The Nyquist rate is the minimum sample rate you need to capture a signal without losing information: twice the signal's highest frequency, or twice its bandwidth for a baseband signal.
If a signal contains frequencies up to 20 kilohertz, its Nyquist rate is 40 kilosamples per second.
That's different from the Nyquist frequency, which is half of whatever sample rate you're actually using, the highest frequency your sampler can represent.
It matters because of what sampling does in the frequency domain: it makes copies of the signal's spectrum centred at multiples of the sample rate.
If you sample faster than twice the highest frequency, the copies don't overlap, and you can recover the original signal exactly with a low-pass filter; that's the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem.
If you sample slower, the copies overlap, high frequencies fold down onto low ones, and that's aliasing, which can't be undone after sampling.

In practice it drives design decisions: you put an anti-alias filter in front of the ADC, you don't sample exactly at the Nyquist rate because real filters can't cut off instantly, so audio goes to 44.
1 or 48 kilohertz for 20 kilohertz content, and many converters oversample so the filter can be simple.
It also sets data rate and power: double the bandwidth and you double the samples you have to move and store."
